newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW - Samsung sets Australia buying spree.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW - Samsung sets Australia buying spree.

text.p: South Korea's giant Samsung Co Ltd group plans one of the biggest commodity-based investment sprees ever in Australia by a foreign company.

After quietly servicing Australia-Korea trade for 21 years, Samsung (Australia) Pty Ltd now plans investment expansion in coal and meat, is looking to become a big wheat producer, wants to set up a A$1 billion gas-based petrochemical plant, and is eyeing gold production and aluminium smelter investments.

It also wants to beclome a major property investor and is considering establishing a A$200 million staff training centre in Australia to teach the group's 200,000 employees what the West is like. But food, energy and metals are the big game.

"We have a firm belief that there will be (an) imbalance in supply and demand in food in the 21st century," Peter (J.G.) Park, managing director of Samsung (Australia) Pty Ltd, said in an interview with Reuters.
Supply shortages were expected to be more serious in Asia in conjunction with the region's very fast growth, he said.
"We are looking into further feasibilities in the agriculture sector (in Australia)," Park said.
While Australian meat producers struggle with low prices, falling demand and uncertainty, Samsung has swooped to become the biggest new meat investor in the country.
In July Samsung invested A$14 million in 5,700 hectares of northern New South Wales (NSW) grazing land and infrastructure.

Also now a coal miner, through its A$120 million half-share in the Springvale coal mine in the Lithgow region of NSW bought three years ago, Samsung (Australia) plans further beef and coal investments if the present ventures are successful.
In coal this would require a minimum further investment of A$200 million by around year 2000.
In meat, opening of the Korean market would make feasible a A$15-A$20 million Australian meatworks investment, Park said.

Meanwhile, the group has feasibility studies underway into investments in grains, forest products, a natural gas-based petrochemical plant and possible gold and aluminium and nickel smelting ventures.
In the belief that grains prices will rise as Asian food demand increases, Samsung is planning a A$20 million investment in a minimum 25,000 acre property on Australia's east coast.

Like the major Japanese trading house Mitsui and Co Ltd, Samsung's interest in becoming a major player in wheat is despite its distaste for export control of Australian wheat by the Australian Wheat Board (AWB).
This may cause Samsung to switch plans from wheat to barley, rice and sorghum. "As for foreigners, it might be a too hectic task (to campaign to change the AWB's monopoly)," Park said.
Investment in a gold mine and a nickel smelter would require a minimum of US$100 million each, while investment in an aluminium smelter would be more than $200 million, Park said.
The planned gold investment would be as a wholly-owned venture, but a move into aluminium was expected to be in an existing smelter, Park said.
He would not name the project.

It is likely, however, that Park was referring to the 45 percent Alcoa of Australia Ltd-owned Portland smelter in Victoria, in which the Victorian state government plans to privatise its 25 percent stake.

Samsung was presently engaged in discussions with the Western Australian government and other "concerned parties" over the planned $1 billion investment in a petrochemical plant, Park said. Again he would not reveal further details.
Park said he believed the majority of the company's big investment plans would come to fruition.

The Seoul-based Samsung group, ranked by Fortune magazine as the 14th biggest company in the world, was willing to finance all of the company's investment plans in Australia, Park said. Again he would not reveal further details.
--Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
